1135.title: Past, present, future mind (section 18)
1135.hook: past mind can't be grasped, present mind can't be grasped, future mind can't be grasped
1135.howItsDone: The line about past, present and future mind is quoted in Chan and Zen teaching, and the story of the monk and the snack seller is told as a teaching tale about it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, suchness: the sutra says the name Tathagata means things just as they are. Your line: suchness. A new week starts.

A story told in the Zen tradition: a learned monk is on the road, his pack full of his own commentaries on the Diamond Sutra. Hungry, he stops at a roadside stall to buy a snack from an old woman. She asks what's in the pack. Notes on the Diamond Sutra, he says. I have a question, she says. Answer it, and the snack is free. The sutra says past mind can't be grasped, present mind can't be grasped, future mind can't be grasped. So which mind is this snack for? He has no answer. Today, the line she quoted.
screen: `A MONK WITH HIS COMMENTARIES.` → `AN OLD WOMAN'S QUESTION.` → `WHICH MIND?`

segments.voice: First, the eyes. Section eighteen opens with short questions. Does the Tathagata have the physical eye? He does, Subhuti says. The heavenly eye? The wisdom eye? The eye of the teaching? The eye of a Buddha? Yes, to each. Five ways of seeing, and the Buddha has every one. Second, the sand. Picture as many rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and as many worlds as there are grains in all those rivers. All the beings in all those worlds, with all their kinds of minds, the Tathagata knows. Third, the turn. Then why does he know them? Because, the sutra says, what are called minds are not minds; that is why they are called minds. The Buddha who sees every mind sees that none is a fixed, solid thing. Fourth, the three. Past mind can't be grasped: it's gone, and what's left is memory, happening now. Future mind can't be grasped: it isn't here yet, and what's here is planning, happening now. Present mind can't be grasped either. Reach for it, and by the time your hand closes, it has moved. That's what silenced the monk. He had studied this line and written about it, but a snack is eaten now, and now can't be caught and held. Some readers hear despair in that. The sutra seems to hear freedom. A mind that can't be grasped also can't be trapped. Yesterday's mistake isn't a cell. Tomorrow's worry isn't a wall. Even this moment's mood is already on its way.

segments.voice: As a breath arrives, try to catch it, to hold this exact instant still, and notice what happens: it's already turning, already leaving. Try again on the next one, without strain; the point isn't to succeed but to feel the moment slip through the fingers, and see whether that feels like loss or like room. When a memory or a plan pulls you away, let it go too.
Past. With present and future, one of the three minds the Diamond Sutra says can't be grasped. Today's word.
Your line: can't be grasped. Not a cell, not a wall: room. A new week, begun.

1136.title: Merit is no merit (section 19)
1136.hook: merit is called merit because it is no fixed thing
1136.howItsDone: In Buddhist communities people make merit by giving to monks and nuns, keeping precepts and supporting teaching, and some dedicate or share that merit with others; Mahayana teachers read section 19 as a reminder not to cling to merit as a possession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, past, present and future mind: none of them can be caught and held. Your line: can't be grasped.

A paper punch card sits in a wallet, nine holes punched, one to go. A child's chore chart on the fridge is crowded with gold stars. An app counts your steps and throws confetti at the goal. We like a tally; there's a pleasure in watching the good add up. Buddhist life has its own word for the good that adds up, and it's an important one: merit. Section nineteen of the Diamond Sutra picks that word up, turns it over once, and sets it down differently.
screen: `A PUNCH CARD, A STAR CHART.` → `WE LIKE A TALLY.` → `THE WORD MERIT.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Merit, in Sanskrit punya, in Pali puñña, is the good that comes from good deeds: giving, keeping precepts, honoring teachers, meditating. In Buddhist communities it's a real and living idea. People give food to monks, light lamps, sponsor a reading, speak of the merit of it, and sometimes share that merit with those who have died. The Diamond Sutra doesn't throw any of that away; it comes back to merit again and again. Second, the question. Once more, a gift on a staggering scale: someone fills a whole vast world system with the seven precious things and gives it all away. Much merit? Very much, Subhuti says. Third, the turn, section nineteen's surprise in one sentence. If merit were a real, solid thing, the Buddha says, the Tathagata would not call it much merit; it's because merit is no fixed thing that he calls it much. The merit isn't denied. Its size isn't denied. What's taken away is the idea that it's a thing you can stack, own, and carry in a pocket. Fourth, the lightness. Some readers hear relief in this. If merit were a pile, you'd have to guard it, compare it, worry about losing it. Because it's so-called merit, a name for the way good spreads out, there's nothing to guard. You can do good and let it go, the way a river doesn't keep the water it passes on. The good is still good. It just isn't yours to count.

1137.title: Not the perfect body (section 20)
1137.hook: the Tathagata isn't seen through a perfect body
1137.howItsDone: Buddhists bow to and make offerings before images of the Buddha; Mahayana teachers use section 20 to say the Buddha is not finally found in a physical form, however perfect.

segments.voice: Yesterday, merit is no merit: the good is real and great, but it's no fixed thing to stack and own. Your line: so-called merit.

At a passport desk, an officer looks at a photo, then at the face in front of him, then back at the photo. The hair is different now; the face is older. In a few seconds he decides the body matches and the person may pass. That's one kind of seeing, and it works well at a border. Section twenty of the Diamond Sutra asks whether it works for a Buddha. If you had stood before the Buddha himself, perfect in form, would that body be where he is seen?
screen: `A PHOTO, A FACE, A MATCH.` → `ONE KIND OF SEEING.` → `IS THAT WHERE HE'S SEEN?`

segments.voice: First, the question. Can the Tathagata be seen through the perfect form of his body? The Sanskrit word for that body is rupakaya, the form-body, the Buddha you could have walked up to and looked at. Second, the answer. No, Subhuti says, because what the Tathagata calls the perfect form-body is not a perfect form-body; that is why it's called the perfect form-body. Then the same question about the marks of a great being, and the same answer: the marks are no marks, and so they're called marks. We've met the marks before; today the weight is on the body itself. Third, what isn't being said. The sutra doesn't say the Buddha had no body, or that his body didn't matter, or that the statues are wrong. In Buddhist homes and temples, images of the Buddha are bowed to, offered flowers, kept with care. The sutra says something narrower and harder: the body isn't where the Tathagata is finally seen. It's a doorway, not the room. Fourth, the mirror. Where are we seen? Usually through a body first: its age, its size, its color, its clothes, how well it's working today. A friend in a hospital bed is not their hospital bed. A grandparent who can't remember your name is not the forgetting. Section twenty doesn't make bodies unimportant. It makes them not the last word.

segments.voice: Feel the body sitting, its weight, an ache somewhere, the face you'd see in a mirror, and notice the verdicts riding along: too tired, too old, not strong enough, fine today. On each out-breath let a verdict soften, and ask quietly who is breathing here, apart from how this body looks or works today. You don't need an answer; let the body be a doorway for a few breaths, not the whole room.

1138.title: Nothing to teach (section 21)
1138.hook: the Tathagata has no teaching to teach; that is called teaching
1138.howItsDone: Some Mahayana teachers frame their own teaching as pointing rather than possessing, and section 21 is read as the Buddha disowning any fixed teaching while still teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not the perfect body: the Tathagata isn't finally seen through the body or its marks. Your line: not the body.

A grandmother kneels on the kitchen floor, teaching a small child to tie a shoe. Two loops. Cross them. Tuck one under. Pull. After a few tries the child gets it and beams. Now, whose knot is that? The grandmother didn't invent it. Someone taught her, and someone taught them. She's passing on something that was never hers, and the child will pass it on without ever saying her name. Section twenty-one of the Diamond Sutra says something like that about the Buddha's own teaching, and then goes further.
screen: `TWO LOOPS, CROSS, TUCK, PULL.` → `WHOSE KNOT IS IT?` → `NEVER HERS TO OWN.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. Don't imagine, the Buddha tells Subhuti, that the Tathagata thinks, I have taught a teaching. Don't even form that idea. Second, the warning. Anyone who says the Tathagata has taught a teaching is misrepresenting him, the sutra says, and hasn't understood what he teaches. That's startling: the voice that has taught all through this sutra refuses the title of the one who taught it. Third, the turn. Why? Because as for teaching the teaching, there is no teaching to be found that could be taught; and that is what is called teaching the teaching. Set that beside a map. You'd be lost without one. But a map isn't the place, and someone who keeps the map and never takes the trip has misunderstood what maps are for. The teaching, in this sutra, is never a possession handed from owner to owner. It's a pointing. Fourth, the question behind. Then Subhuti asks something tender. In ages to come, will there be beings who hear a teaching like this and trust it? The Buddha answers in the sutra's way: they are not beings, nor are they not beings. The ones who will hear it can't be counted as fixed selves either. The teaching passes through people the way a knot passes through hands. Nobody owns the knot, and yet every time it's tied right, a shoe stays on. The Buddha teaches, fully and carefully, and lets go of owning what he taught.

1139.title: Nothing gained (section 22)
1139.hook: in the highest awakening, not even the least thing is gained
1139.howItsDone: In some Zen teaching, practice is described as sitting without a gaining mind, not trying to acquire anything; section 22 is read as supporting this.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nothing to teach: the Buddha teaches fully, then refuses to own what he taught. Your line: no teaching, teaching.

So, what did you get out of it? It's a question that follows people home from all sorts of things: a weekend away, a class, a hard year, a long talk with a friend. We want to point at something we're carrying back, a skill, a lesson, a photo, a certificate. Section twenty-two of the Diamond Sutra puts that question to the Buddha's own awakening, and the answer, in his own words, is startling.
screen: `WHAT DID YOU GET OUT OF IT?` → `SOMETHING TO CARRY BACK.` → `ASKED OF AWAKENING ITSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the size. Section twenty-two is only a few lines long. No sands of the Ganges, no worlds of treasure, just a question and an answer, like the moment in a long conversation when someone finally says the plain thing. Second, the question. When you reached the highest, most complete awakening, Subhuti asks, was it that you reached nothing? He isn't being cheeky. He's been listening all through this sutra, and he's drawing the line out to its end. Third, the answer. So it is, Subhuti, so it is, the Buddha says, the words doubled as if to make sure nobody softens them. In that highest awakening, not even the least thing is found or gained, and that is what is called the highest, most complete awakening. The Sanskrit is anuttara samyak sambodhi: awakening with nothing above it, whole and right. Its wholeness, the sutra claims, comes from there being nothing in it to hold. Fourth, an ordinary day. If awakening isn't a thing acquired, it can't be stacked on a shelf with other accomplishments, or lost, or compared. One way to picture it: less like buying a lamp, more like opening the curtains. The light was never something you owned. What changes is what's no longer in the way. This doesn't make practice pointless. The Buddha practiced, and the sutra keeps urging people to keep and recite it. It only means practice isn't a purchase. You can work hard at something and still not need to walk away holding it.

1140.title: Equal, no high or low (section 23)
1140.hook: this truth is level; there is nothing high or low in it
1140.howItsDone: Mahayana teachers read section 23 as saying awakening holds no ranks: good deeds are done without the ideas of self, person, being or life-span, and without making goodness a way to stand higher.

A carpenter sets a spirit level on a new shelf. The little bubble drifts, wobbles, and settles dead center between the two lines. Level. Nothing sloping toward one end, nothing tipping the other way. Section twenty-three of the Diamond Sutra uses a word a carpenter would understand. It says the truth it has been circling is level, even, and then says what that means for anyone who walks on it.
screen: `A BUBBLE SETTLES CENTER.` → `NOTHING TIPS.` → `A LEVEL TRUTH.`

segments.voice: First, the word. This teaching is equal, the Buddha tells Subhuti, and there is nothing high or low in it; that is what is called the highest, most complete awakening. The Sanskrit word for equal is sama: same, even, level. Second, the paradox. The awakening the sutra keeps calling highest has no high and no low inside it. It's highest precisely because it isn't a ladder, with no top rung for someone to stand on while others wait below. Third, how it's reached. Without the idea of a self, a person, a being, or a life-span, by doing all good things, one awakens. Those four ideas have come up again and again in this sutra; here they're named again as what has to fall away. It doesn't say do nothing. It says do all good things, without building a self on top of them. Fourth, the last twist. These good things, the Buddha adds, are called by the Tathagata not good things; that is why they are called good things. Even goodness isn't allowed to become a rank. The moment good deeds become a way of standing above someone, they've stopped being level. In ordinary life we live inside heights: job titles, seating charts, who speaks first at the table, who gets thanked by name. The sutra doesn't pretend those disappear. It says that underneath them, in what's truest, there's nothing to climb.

1141.title: Heaps of jewels (section 24)
1141.hook: jewels piled high as mountains are less than keeping four lines
1141.howItsDone: In some Mahayana communities people memorize and chant verses of the Diamond Sutra, and teach them to others, which the sutra names as a way of keeping it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, equal: the teaching is level, with nothing high or low in it. Your line: no high, no low.

A woman leaves her bag on a train: wallet, phone, keys, the ring she took off to wash her hands. Gone. That night, unable to sleep, she finds herself saying a poem she learned as a girl, every line still there. The train took everything she carried in her hands. It couldn't touch what she carried by heart. Section twenty-four of the Diamond Sutra sets those two kinds of keeping side by side, and it doesn't hold back on the size of the pile.
screen: `A BAG LEFT ON A TRAIN.` → `A POEM STILL THERE.` → `TWO KINDS OF KEEPING.`

segments.voice: First, the heap. Someone piles up the seven precious things, gold, silver and the rest, in heaps as high as all the Sumeru mountains in a vast world system, and gives them all away. Sumeru, in Buddhist cosmology, is the great mountain at the center of a world, so this is a gift the size of a mountain range, made of treasure. Second, the four lines. Someone else takes this teaching of the perfection of wisdom, even just four lines of it, keeps it, recites it, and explains it to others. That's all. Third, the scale. The merit of the mountain of jewels, the Buddha says, is not a hundredth part of the merit of the four lines. Not the tiniest share, not any fraction you could name or compare. The sutra pushes the numbers until numbers give up. Fourth, why. We've heard this comparison before, but today's picture makes the reason plain. Jewels are given once, and then they're gone, or lost, or fought over. Four lines kept by heart travel with a person through sleepless nights and hospital waiting rooms, and when they're explained to someone else, nobody has less. All week the sutra has been taking things away: no grasping the mind, no merit to own, no perfect body, nothing to teach, nothing gained, no high or low. Then it hands back something small enough to carry anywhere: a few lines, by heart.
screen: `JEWELS HIGH AS SUMERU.` · `FOUR LINES, KEPT AND SHARED.` · `NOT A HUNDREDTH PART.` · `WHAT A TRAIN CAN'T TAKE.` · then, large: `LESS THAN FOUR LINES.`

segments.voice: Here are four of this week's lines: can't be grasped, so-called merit, not the least thing, no high, no low. Say one silently on each out-breath, in order, then try them again without help; if one slips, wait a breath and let it come back on its own, and if it doesn't, that's all right. Go round again, a little slower, until they're yours to carry without a page.
Heaps of jewels. In section twenty-four, treasure piled as high as mountains gives less merit than keeping and sharing four lines of this teaching. Today's word.
